opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that reinforcement learning is learning from the consequences of your own actions, rather than from someone telling you the right answer.

In supervised learning, you're given an input and a label, and you imitate it. That's powerful, but it puts a ceiling on you: you can only get as good as the data you're copying. Reinforcement learning is different. You act in the world, something happens, you get some signal, maybe a reward, maybe just "that worked" or "that didn't," and you adjust. No one shows you the optimal move. You discover it.

That's why I find it such a natural description of how people get better. Think about learning to ride a bike, or learning to negotiate, or even learning research taste. Nobody can hand you the correct trajectory. You try something, you fall, you notice what led to the fall, and slowly your policy improves. The key ingredients are all there: you need to explore, because if you only do what you already know, you never find anything better. You need a reward signal that actually reflects what you care about. And you need credit assignment, figuring out which of the many things you did actually caused the outcome. That last part is hard, for algorithms and for humans. When something goes well in your life, was it the decision you made yesterday, or one you made three years ago?

Another point I find interesting is the tension between exploration and exploitation. Early on you should be willing to try many things, even things that look worse in the short term, because the information is valuable. Later you can exploit what you've learned. A lot of people, and a lot of systems, exploit too early. They find something that works okay and stop searching.

For large models specifically, what's exciting right now is that RL lets a model go beyond imitating human text. If you can define a verifiable goal, solving a math problem, passing tests in code, completing a task, the model can practice, fail, and improve on its own experience. That's a qualitatively different kind of learning. It's less "read everything humans wrote" and more "go out and practice." And practice is how you get past the teacher.

So to me, RL is really a formalization of a very old idea: experience is the teacher, but only if you have a good way to tell good outcomes from bad ones, and the courage to explore.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it, reinforcement learning is really the closest thing we have to a formal theory of learning from experience, and the key word there is experience, not instruction.

With supervised learning, someone hands you the right answer. You see an image, you're told it's a cat, you adjust. But most of what we actually learn in life doesn't come with labels. Nobody tells a child the correct motor command for walking. You try something, you fall, you try something slightly different, and over thousands of attempts a kind of competence emerges. Reinforcement learning is the attempt to capture exactly that loop: act, observe the consequence, update, act again.

What I find deep about it is that the feedback is often sparse and delayed. You might make a hundred decisions and only find out at the end whether the whole sequence worked. So the hard problem isn't just "did I do well," it's "which of those hundred decisions deserve the credit or the blame." That's the credit assignment problem, and I'd argue it's the central intellectual question of the whole field. It's also, if you think about it, a very human question. We spend a lot of our lives trying to figure out which of our past choices actually mattered.

The other piece is exploration. If you only ever do what has worked before, you get stuck. You have to deliberately try things that might be worse, in order to find out whether they're better. That tension between exploiting what you know and exploring what you don't is, to me, the real meaning of "becoming better through experience." It's not just accumulating experience. It's being willing to have the right kinds of experiences, including the uncomfortable ones.

And I'd add one more thing. In the last few years, the field has shifted. We used to think of RL as something you did from scratch, in a game or a simulator. Now the most interesting applications start with a model that already knows a great deal, from language, from reading, and RL is the stage where that knowledge gets tested against reality and sharpened. That feels much closer to how expertise actually develops in people. You read, you study, and then at some point you have to go do the thing, and the doing teaches you something the reading never could.

astra-6.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as learning through a loop: you take an action, you see what happens, and you adjust what you do next. Rather than being told the correct answer every time, you get feedback about how well things went.

Imagine learning to ride a bicycle. You try a movement, feel yourself wobble, and make an adjustment. Over time, those experiences help you develop a better way of balancing. In reinforcement learning, we call that way of choosing actions a policy.

What makes it interesting is that a good action doesn’t always pay off immediately. Sometimes you have to try something unfamiliar or accept a short-term cost to get a better result later. So becoming better through experience means learning which actions lead to good outcomes over time—and that depends a lot on whether the feedback rewards what you actually want to achieve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as learning through a loop: you act, you see what happens, and you adjust. Instead of being told the correct answer at every step, you receive feedback—a reward—that helps you discover which actions lead to better outcomes.

The interesting part is that better outcomes may take time. An action that feels rewarding immediately might hurt you later, while something difficult now might pay off in the future. So learning means connecting your choices to their longer-term consequences.

You also have to balance using what already works with trying something new. If you never explore, you may never discover a better approach. Experience helps you improve when you use that feedback to change what you do next.
